Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) is introduced to enhance the representation of curved crest-line structures, while the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) strengthens responses to low-contrast ISW features. A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea was constructed for model training and evaluation. YOLO11-ISW achieved detection Precision, Recall, and F1-score values of 92.01%, 80.73%, and 86.00%, respectively, and segmentation values of 93.14%, 82.60%, and 87.55%, respectively. The model achieved the highest detection and segmentation F1-scores among the evaluated methods. The segmentation results were further georeferenced to extract ISW crest-line locations, and the framework was applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020 to investigate satellite-observed ISW spatiotemporal variability. The detected ISWs exhibited pronounced spatial clustering, strong spring–summer seasonality, and clear lunar-cycle modulation, consistent with previous observations in the northern South China Sea. These results demonstrate the potential of YOLO11-ISW for automated, long-term, and large-scale monitoring of ISWs using satellite remote sensing imagery.

The paper that matters most for the Marine heatwave early warning project is **#4 — "Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish"** (Stuart-Smith et al., 2026, Conservation Science and Practice).

**Why it leads the slate:**

- **It's the clearest demonstration of your project's end goal.** Your project is about *early warning* — not just predicting marine heatwaves, but acting on the prediction before the event hits. #4 is a real, documented case where a forecast of an extreme event (the 2023/2024 El Niño MHW) triggered a pre-emptive rescue of a critically endangered species. The forecast → decision → action chain is exactly what an early warning system is for.

- **It gives you a concrete evaluation framework.** The paper shows what "good enough" looks like: the forecast identified >20°C or +~3°C extremes ahead of time, an expert workshop judged the threat, and the intervention was timed so the fish were out of the water before in-situ temperatures exceeded records (80 days more than 2°C above the long-term mean). That's a template for how your lab's forecasts could be operationalized.

- **It's a conservation-relevance anchor.** For grant writing and stakeholder engagement (coastal managers, fisheries, conservation bodies), this is the paper that makes the "so what" obvious. It's also Australia's first pre-emptive rescue of a protected marine species, which gives it weight in any proposal or briefing.

**The other papers are useful but secondary:**
- **#5** (ML MHW forecasts, Bay of Bengal) is methodologically relevant to your ML-for-data-assimilation interest, but it's a B.S. thesis evaluation against persistence benchmarks — a useful benchmarking reference, not a direction-setter.
- **#8** (Rescene-ESM) is interesting for the ML-coupled-climate-model angle, but it's about Earth system modeling at century scales, not operational early warning.
- **#10** (Pacific Regional Ocean Forecast System) is a data product, not a method or application paper.

If you want, I can pull the full text of #4 and walk through the forecast-to-action timeline in detail, or check how #4 and #5 fit against the GEO Core grant (#6) that's also on the slate.

#4 [paper] Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish
Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly
Venue: Conservation Science and Practice
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/csp2.70439
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.

#8 [paper] Rescene-ESM: an Earth system model built around a frozen AI weather model
Authors: Minjong Cheon, Kaoru Kakinuma
Year: 2026
Link: https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/e1c22d8441861158dd7f9e6021cb718096d3f29f

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The high computational cost of Earth system models limits the exploration of scenarios and ensemble members, while existing machine-learning weather models coupled to oceans have produced weak El Niño variability or relied on climate-model output, and none effectively routes climate impacts through…
Method (Mycelium's reading): Rescene-ESM, an Earth system model using a coupler named YAHO that links a frozen 20.8-million-parameter AI weather model to physically formulated ocean, sea-ice, land, river, carbon, and energy components constrained by observations; the model uses an interactive mixed layer, an equatorial wave oc…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Simulations of approximately 1,000 years on one graphics processing unit; evaluation against observed climate data from 1979-2022; routing of runoff to 212 river gauges; and future projections for SSP1 and SSP3 scenarios for the period 2081-2100.
Abstract:
Earth system models underpin climate projections, but their cost limits how many scenarios, ensemble members and impact pathways can be explored. Machine-learning weather models forecast as skillfully as physics-based models at a fraction of the cost, yet coupled to an ocean they have produced weak El Nino variability or have learned it from climate-model output, and none carries the climate through rivers to the people exposed to it. Here we present Rescene-ESM, an Earth system model whose coupler, YAHO, yokes a frozen 20.8-million-parameter AI weather model to physically formulated ocean, sea-ice, land, river, carbon and energy components constrained by observations. Adding the couplings one at a time shows what each contributes: over a climatological ocean the AI atmosphere varies from year to year by a third of the observed amount over the oceans, and an interactive mixed layer, an equatorial wave ocean, the residual of the observed sea surface temperature (SST) equation as stochastic forcing and the land's moisture flux raise this step by step and bring El Nino and its teleconnections, leaving the mean climate almost unchanged. The full model simulates about 1,000 years per day on one graphics processing unit, holds the observed climate for a thousand years without drift, reproduces the observed 1979-2022 global warming, carries forced change with a physically based structure around the frozen network (transient climate response 1.60 K), routes runoff to 212 river gauges with a median seasonal-cycle correlation of 0.79 and, driven by emissions, separates the heatwave exposure of an SSP1 and an SSP3 world by a factor of 4.7 in 2081-2100, three-quarters of it through the warmer climate.

Authors: Guocai Rong, Huanhe Dong, Yuan Kong, Ze Liu, Yong Hui Fang
Venue: Remote Sensing
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3390/rs18213843
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Automated extraction of internal solitary waves (ISWs) from satellite imagery is challenging due to their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast.
Method (Mycelium's reading): YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint detection and pixel-level segmentation, incorporating Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) for curved structures and the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) for low-contrast features.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea; the framework was also applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020.
Abstract:
Internal solitary waves (ISWs) play an important role in ocean energy transport and mixing, yet their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast make automated extraction from satellite imagery challenging. To address these challenges, this study proposes YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint ISW detection and pixel-level segmentation. Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) is introduced to enhance the representation of curved crest-line structures, while the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) strengthens responses to low-contrast ISW features. A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea was constructed for model training and evaluation. YOLO11-ISW achieved detection Precision, Recall, and F1-score values of 92.01%, 80.73%, and 86.00%, respectively, and segmentation values of 93.14%, 82.60%, and 87.55%, respectively. The model achieved the highest detection and segmentation F1-scores among the evaluated methods. The segmentation results were further georeferenced to extract ISW crest-line locations, and the framework was applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020 to investigate satellite-observed ISW spatiotemporal variability. The detected ISWs exhibited pronounced spatial clustering, strong spring–summer seasonality, and clear lunar-cycle modulation, consistent with previous observations in the northern South China Sea. These results demonstrate the potential of YOLO11-ISW for automated, long-term, and large-scale monitoring of ISWs using satellite remote sensing imagery.

final_text:
Here's the comparison, grounded in what each grant asks for and what the Marine heatwave early warning project (#3) is doing.

## The two grants at a glance

| | **#1 – Stronger GOOS** | **#2 – Antarctica & Southern Ocean** |
|---|---|---|
| Amount | €50,000,000 | €5,000,000–€11,000,000 |
| Deadline | 2027-02-16 | 2027-09-23 |
| Core ask | Strengthen the *global observing system*: deploy equipment, run observing-system (sim) experiments, network optimisation, co-create tech roadmaps with industry | Resolve uncertainties and improve *projections* of the Antarctic/Southern Ocean; ocean–atmosphere–sea-ice–ice-sheet interactions; ESMs and regional coupled models; monitoring indicators |
| Setting | Global, with emphasis on areas beyond national jurisdiction, polar regions, deep sea | Antarctic continental shelves, bottom-water formation regions |

## Which fits the project better

**#2 (Antarctica & Southern Ocean) is the closer fit**, for three reasons:

1. **Method match.** The project's slate is full of *forecasting and model-evaluation* work — ML-based 1–14-day marine heatwave forecasts benchmarked against persistence (#7), daily analyses of a regional ocean forecast system (#12), and an Earth-system model built around an AI weather model (#10). #2 explicitly calls for "improving Earth System Models (ESMs) and regional coupled models" and resolving projection uncertainties, including "extreme events." That is the same muscle the project is flexing.

2. **Problem match.** #2 is about *understanding and projecting* ocean change and extremes. The project is about *predicting* marine heatwaves. #1, by contrast, is about the *infrastructure* of observation — deploying equipment, governance, network optimisation, EU strategic autonomy. That's a systems/infrastructure problem, not a forecasting one.

3. **Scale realism.** #2's €5–11M is a size a 3-member lab project can plausibly lead or anchor. #1's €50M is a consortium-scale call that would need a much broader observing-network partner base.

## The honest caveats

- **Region.** #2 is specifically Antarctic/Southern Ocean. If the project's heatwave work is centred elsewhere (e.g. the Bay of Bengal, #7, or the Pacific, #12), the *method* still matches but you'd need to frame the contribution as Southern Ocean–relevant or as a regional method that generalises. Worth checking where the project's active work sits before committing.
- **Neither grant is a perfect "marine heatwave" call.** Both are broader climate/ocean calls where heatwave prediction is one component. #2 just gives that component more room.
- I couldn't open the project's full state (goals, method, blockers) in this conversation — the detail above is from the project's current slate (#3) and the two grant texts. If you can share the project's stated method/goals, I can sharpen the fit call.

**Bottom line:** lead with **#2** — it rewards the forecasting/modeling work the project is already doing, at a scale the lab can carry. Keep **#1** in view only if you want to anchor the project's *data/observation* side within a larger GOOS consortium.

Want me to draft a short fit statement for #2 you could use in the application, or check who in the lab is best positioned to lead it?

#10 [paper] Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish
Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly
Venue: Conservation Science and Practice
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/csp2.70439
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.

final_text:
Here's what I found, in three parts.

## Best-fit open grant

**#3 Green, circular and resilient harbours** (Horizon, Mission "Restore our Ocean and Waters") — still open, deadline **21 Sep 2027**, €1M–€8.9M.

Why it fits the Plastic pathways project (#2) best:
- The call asks for place-based, people-centred actions that **prevent and eliminate pollution of our ocean, seas and waters** and make the blue economy circular — that is exactly the debris-pathways problem your lab works on (marine litter tracking, forecasting where floating debris ends up).
- It explicitly wants **scientific partners alongside port authorities and local stakeholders**, and it covers all four sea basins — so a modelling/forecasting group can slot in as the science arm of a multi-port consortium.
- The deadline (Sep 2027) gives you a full year to build the consortium, which matters because the call requires demonstration in **at least 4 ports, one in each basin** — that's the biggest lift.

The other open candidates fit less well:
- **#4 ZEWAT waterborne transport** (deadline 14 Apr 2027) is about pollution from *zero-carbon fuels and spills* — a different pollution source than plastic pathways.
- **#8 biotech recycling of complex plastics** (deadline 22 Sep 2027) is a materials/biotech topic (enzymes, microbes, TRL 4–5) — far from your lab's method.
- **#20 Microplastics Research and Resource Coordination Center** (deadline **1 Dec 2026**, ~3 weeks away) is the closest in subject, but it's a US NIEHS U24 coordination center for *health effects* of micro/nanoplastics — a biomedical framing, and the timeline is very tight.
- The project's current slate (#23, #24, #25, #26, #27) is all ocean-observation/infrastructure topics — none is about debris.

**Biggest doubt on #3:** it is a Mission topic that expects port authorities and public bodies as core partners and a 4-basin demonstration — you'd be joining an existing consortium structure, not writing a pure research proposal.

## Who in the lab should lead

**Jonah Whitcombe (#15)** — he's the only member who declares **marine litter** and **Lagrangian analysis**, which is the core of the Plastic pathways project, and he's already a project member. He'd be the natural scientific lead.

**Priya Raman (#16)** is the natural second: her declared **satellite oceanography** and **coastal water quality** map directly onto the monitoring and pollution-reduction work the call expects.

You (#14) would anchor it as PI of the lab and lead the consortium-building side. The nightly ranking agrees: Jonah is the closest profile match for #3, then Priya.

One honest caveat: the call's required roles — **port managing authorities and public administrations** — are not covered by anyone's declared profile in the lab. That's the gap you'd fill with partners.

## Who outside the lab to partner with

I can't name specific people here: collaborator search is turned off on this instance, and I found no co-authorship path to anyone you can see that I could verify. So I'll say what the call *requires* rather than guess at names:

- **Port authorities / public bodies** in at least four basins (Atlantic & Arctic, Mediterranean, Baltic & North Sea, Danube incl. Black Sea) — the call strongly encourages them as consortium partners, and they're the missing role in your lab.
- **Local coastal stakeholders and industry partners** (fishing, marinas, commercial ports) for the place-based actions.
- A **marine-litter or debris-removal research group** to complement your forecasting strength, if your consortium doesn't already have one.

If you'd like, I can dig into any of the other open calls in more detail, or look at what's in the project's slate (#23–#27) to see if any of those observation topics could be bundled into a broader application.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The decarbonization of waterborne transport using renewable low and zero-carbon fuels introduces new, unexplored risks to marine and aquatic ecosystems, including pollution from normal operations and accidental spills, threatening the achievement of Good Environmental and Ecological Status in Europ…
Method (Mycelium's reading): The project aims to evaluate and forecast environmental impacts, model pollution sources, and develop, demonstrate, and test innovative prevention, abatement, and mitigation systems and strategies (targeting TRL 5) for managing spills and reducing harmful impacts of zero-emission fuels.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): European marine waters, inland waterways, and port areas, focusing on waterborne transport operations using renewable low and zero-carbon fuels.
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes.

- Improved water resilience and good environmental and good ecological status in European waters and contribute to the achievement of the European Union's environmental targets, including the European Water Resilience Strategy and the European Ocean Pact.

- A comprehensive understanding of the future environmental impacts of waterborne transport on marine and other aquatic ecosystems, addressing in particular pollution sources from: i) navigation on renewable low and zero-carbon fuels; and ii) accidental spills of renewable low and zero-carbon fuels for marine waters, inland waters and ports (water and air quality).

- Innovative prevention, abatement and mitigation systems and strategies for reducing and eliminating the harmful impacts of waterborne transport on waters.

- Enhanced pollution prevention and mitigation in marine waters, inland waterways and port areas, reducing the likelihood and impact of accidents involving renewable low and zero-carbon fuels.

Scope:

The European Union aims to protect and conserve its marine and freshwater environments by achieving Good Environmental and Good Ecological Status[1]. The European Water Resilience Strategy and the European Ocean Pact further emphasize the need to enhance the resilience of European waters to human-induced pressures. Projects like the Horizon Europe EMERGE have researched the impacts of shipping on marine ecosystems. The introduction of technologies to decarbonize the sector may enable, to a certain extent, to phase-out relevant current sources of water and air pollution. However, renewable low and zero-carbon fuels and procedures pose new risks to marine and other aquatic ecosystems like rivers and lakes yet to be explored and addressed, both from the normal function of waterborne transport[2] and from accidental spills of renewable low and zero-carbon fuels. In addition, other pollution sources can be addressed today[3]. This topic aims to evaluate, forecast, control and mitigate the impact of waterborne transport on marine and other aquatic ecosystems, with a focus on developing and demonstrating innovative abatement and mitigation systems and strategies to mitigate and eliminate, where possible, the harmful impact of waterborne transport in the ocean and inland waters. Actions should address all of the following aspects:

The proposal may include testing and experimental work in relation with spills.

- Develop and demonstrate effective response scenarios, including the associated abatement technologies and any potential new innovative equipment, for managing uncontrolled releases of renewable low and zero-carbon fuels in marine and inland waters or in port areas, including dedicated specific procedures and operational guidelines.

final_text:
Here's the picture for **Plastic pathways** (#2):

## Where the project stands

The project has three members — Jonah Whitcombe, Priya Raman, and you. However, Mycelium holds no confirmed state for it: no goals, method, stage, milestones, or blockers are recorded, and I can't see when it was last reviewed. That means this summary may be out of date — if the team has made progress, it isn't reflected in the project record yet. You can update the project's state in the app.

## Three most relevant new papers

All three entered the slate this week (2026-11-10):

1. **#4 — "A tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter"** (Lim & Hong, 2026, Zenodo). The most directly on-point item: a three-phase beaching kernel plus six particle kernels for OceanParcels 3.1.4, validated against field records from Uido, Korea, using ROMS flow fields. This is essentially a ready-made methodological building block for tracking how plastic moves and beaches — the core of your project.

2. **#3 — "Daily Analyses of the Pacific Regional Ocean Forecast System model"** (Zhang, 2026, Zenodo). A data release of daily analyses from a regional ocean forecast system. Relevant as a potential flow-field / forcing source for particle-tracking experiments, in the same spirit as the ROMS fields used in #4.

3. **#7 — "A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery"** (Rong et al., 2026, Remote Sensing). Less central, but useful as a template for automated satellite-based detection of ocean features — the same kind of ML pipeline you'd apply to spotting debris plumes or aggregates in imagery.

The other new papers on the slate (#6 multi-agent tracking, #10 satellite imagery in human rights, #11 lake hydroclimatology) are only tangentially related.

## One funding opportunity to consider

**#9 — "A stronger Global Ocean Observing System to enhance Europe's strategic autonomy, climate resilience and biodiversity conservation"** (Horizon Europe, €50,000,000; deadline 2027-02-16).

Why it fits: the call explicitly funds observing-system experiments, network optimisation, and the deployment of observation equipment for marine biodiversity and ecosystem knowledge, with attention to under-observed regions. A plastic-pathways project — which needs to track where debris goes and how it affects ecosystems — can be framed as an observing-system contribution: combining in-situ and satellite observations to close gaps in how we monitor marine pollution. It's the best match of the three grants on the slate (#5 is US-focused instrumentation development; #8 and #12 are space-sector technology calls aimed at TRL 4–8, a stretch for a research-lab project).

**Suggested next steps:**
- Confirm the project's current state in the app (goals, method, blockers) so Mylo can tie future slate items to specific blockers.
- If #4's beaching kernel looks usable, the team could pull the code and test it against a local flow field — that would be a concrete first development to record.
- If the #9 call interests you, I can run a fuller grant-fit assessment against the project's confirmed state once it's updated.

#7 [paper] A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery over the Northern South China Sea
Authors: Guocai Rong, Huanhe Dong, Yuan Kong, Ze Liu, Yong Hui Fang
Venue: Remote Sensing
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3390/rs18213843
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Automated extraction of internal solitary waves (ISWs) from satellite imagery is challenging due to their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast.
Method (Mycelium's reading): YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint detection and pixel-level segmentation, incorporating Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) for curved structures and the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) for low-contrast features.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea; the framework was also applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020.
Abstract:
Internal solitary waves (ISWs) play an important role in ocean energy transport and mixing, yet their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast make automated extraction from satellite imagery challenging. To address these challenges, this study proposes YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint ISW detection and pixel-level segmentation. Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) is introduced to enhance the representation of curved crest-line structures, while the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) strengthens responses to low-contrast ISW features. A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea was constructed for model training and evaluation. YOLO11-ISW achieved detection Precision, Recall, and F1-score values of 92.01%, 80.73%, and 86.00%, respectively, and segmentation values of 93.14%, 82.60%, and 87.55%, respectively. The model achieved the highest detection and segmentation F1-scores among the evaluated methods. The segmentation results were further georeferenced to extract ISW crest-line locations, and the framework was applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020 to investigate satellite-observed ISW spatiotemporal variability. The detected ISWs exhibited pronounced spatial clustering, strong spring–summer seasonality, and clear lunar-cycle modulation, consistent with previous observations in the northern South China Sea. These results demonstrate the potential of YOLO11-ISW for automated, long-term, and large-scale monitoring of ISWs using satellite remote sensing imagery.

#10 [paper] Building Consensus on Satellite Imagery in Human Rights Investigations across Epistemic Communities: Insights from Journalism and Law
Authors: Myriam Redondo-Escudero, Yvonne McDermott
Venue: Human Rights Review
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1007/s12142-026-00776-z
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The alignment of practices and identification of shared challenges in the use of satellite imagery for human rights investigations across different epistemic communities (media, NGOs, and courts).
Method (Mycelium's reading): Analysis of data from a survey and legal documents to explore the alignment of practices from media and NGOs to courts.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Journalists, human rights practitioners, and international criminal law contexts involving satellite imagery.
Abstract:
Abstract Satellite imagery has gained a paramount role in human rights investigations. Once the preserve of state intelligence agencies, the increase of commercially-available satellite imagery in recent years has enabled a broader range of actors to analyze earth observation data as part of their investigations. Investigative journalists were at the forefront of incorporating these techniques, with human rights organizations and international tribunals now utilizing satellite imagery as evidence of atrocity crimes. This article explores the alignment of practices from media and NGOs to courts, in order to discern best practices and shared challenges. Drawing on both data from a survey and legal documents, it provides unique perspectives from journalists and human rights practitioners working with satellite imagery and offers key insights from international criminal law. It explores issues around access to data; verification and preservation procedures, and the risks of misinterpretation and gaps. The article ends with recommendations mainly focused on three key facets of satellite imagery: understanding the source; verifying the imagery, and preserving the evidence.

#11 [paper] Temporal completeness reveals long-term hydroclimatic trend reversal: a multi-temporal remote sensing assessment of Lake Belevi (Türkiye), 2000–2026
Authors: Nazif Güler, Müge AĞCA, Zeynel Abidin Polat
Venue: Theoretical and Applied Climatology
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1007/s00704-026-06722-w
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Satellite-based monitoring studies often end before recent severe droughts, potentially biasing long-term trend assessments of Mediterranean freshwater systems.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A 26-year (January 2000–April 2026) hydroclimatic assessment using 273 monthly Landsat-derived surface water observations integrated with CHIRPS precipitation, ERA5 temperature, and watershed NDVI within Google Earth Engine; analysis included seasonal Mann–Kendall trend tests and PELT change-point …
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Lake Belevi (İzmir, Türkiye), 2000–2026.
Abstract:
Abstract Climate-induced hydrological change increasingly threatens Mediterranean freshwater systems, yet many satellite-based monitoring studies end before the recent sequence of severe droughts, potentially biasing long-term trend assessments. This study presents a temporally complete 26-year (January 2000–April 2026) hydroclimatic assessment of Lake Belevi (İzmir, Türkiye) using 273 monthly Landsat-derived surface water observations integrated with CHIRPS precipitation, ERA5 temperature, and watershed NDVI within Google Earth Engine. Seasonal Mann–Kendall analysis of the full series revealed a significant decreasing trend (p = 0.014, Sen slope = − 1.27 ha month⁻¹), whereas the truncated 2000–2020 record showed a significant increasing trend (p = 0.008), suggesting that extending observations beyond recent droughts can change the inferred direction of long-term hydrological trends. PELT detection identified five hydrological regime shifts (2005, 2013, 2016, 2022, and 2025), while the 2025 drought reduced lake area to 4.7 ha (96.5% below the 2013–2016 peak), followed by rapid recovery to 180.7 ha by February 2026. Watershed NDVI increased significantly (+ 53.2%, p < 0.001) despite declining water extent. These findings indicate that temporally truncated satellite records may underestimate drought-induced hydrological degradation and even reverse the inferred direction of long-term trends, supporting more robust climate-change attribution and adaptive water-resource management.

Here's the picture across both projects. One honest caveat up front: I couldn't open the two project records directly (Mycelium wouldn't let me), so I'm working from the lab's current slate and the deadline list, which is where the urgency shows.

## The two most urgent deadlines

**1. Manuscript — 10th World Conference on Computing and Communication Technologies — due 2026-11-15 (2 days)**
This is the lab's most urgent item, and it's the one that fits the **Marine heatwave early warning** project.
- **Who fits:** The nightly ranking names **Tomás Ferreira-Lind** (circulation and turbulence, physics-informed ML) and **you** (data assimilation with ML, ocean extremes) for the heatwave/forecasting papers in the slate. Tomás is the natural lead on the ML-forecasting content; you'd anchor the data-assimilation framing.
- **Paper that would strengthen it:** **#42 "Depth-Resolved Marine Heatwave Prediction in the Levantine Basin"** — ML and explainable-AI MHW prediction, the top-ranked new paper in the slate, and the one the ranking points at Tomás and you. It's a 2026 result that would give the manuscript a current, citable methodological anchor. (If you want a broader global-scale reference, #34 Ocean-E2E is the other strong 2026 option — hybrid physics/data-driven 40-day MHW forecasting with end-to-end neural assimilation.)

**2. Manuscript — 10th International Conference on Geoinformatics and Data Analysis — due 2026-11-20 (7 days)**
This is the next most urgent, and it's the one that fits the **Plastic pathways** project.
- **Who fits:** **Jonah Whitcombe** (marine litter, Lagrangian analysis) is the clear lead — the ranking names him for the marine-litter particle-tracking papers. **Priya Raman** (satellite oceanography, coastal water quality) is a good second for the observation/monitoring angle.
- **Paper that would strengthen it:** **#48 "A tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter"** (Lim & Hong, 2026) — a particle-tracking beaching kernel for OceanParcels applied to field records, which the ranking names for Jonah, Priya and you. It's a direct methodological match for a pathways/deposition manuscript. (A complementary observation-grounded reference is #28, the Mediterranean Lagrangian particle-tracking study, if you want to cite an observation-anchored transport framework.)

#34 [paper] Ocean-E2E: Hybrid Physics-Based and Data-Driven Global Forecasting of Marine Heatwaves with End-to-End Neural Assimilation
Authors: Ruiqi Shu, Ruijian Gou, Yanfei Xiang, Xiaomeng Huang
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1145/3770855.3818893
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This work focuses on the end-to-end forecast of global extreme marine heatwaves (MHWs), which are unusually warm sea surface temperature events with profound impacts on marine ecosystems. Accurate prediction of extreme MHWs has significant scientific and financial worth. However, existing methods still have certain limitations in forecasting general patterns and extreme events. In this study, to address these issues, based on the physical nature of MHWs, we created a novel hybrid data-driven and numerical MHWs forecast framework Ocean-E2E, which is capable of 40-day accurate MHW forecasting with end-to-end data assimilation. Our framework significantly improves the forecast ability of MHWs by explicitly modeling the effect of oceanic mesoscale advection and air-sea interaction based on a dynamic kernel. Furthermore, Ocean-E2E is capable of end-to-end MHWs forecast and regional high-resolution prediction, allowing our framework to operate completely independently of numerical models while outperforming the current state-of-the-art ocean numerical/AI forecasting-assimilation models. Experimental results show that the proposed framework performs excellently on global-to-regional scales and short-to-long-term forecasts, especially in those most extreme MHWs. Overall, our model provides a framework for forecasting and understanding MHWs and other climate extremes. The source code is available at https://github.com/ChiyodaMomo01/Ocean-E2E.

#28 [paper] Marine litter in the Mediterranean: observation-based Lagrangian particle tracking
Authors: Santiago Bravo, Eugenia Pasanisi, Svitlana Liubartseva, Giovanni Coppini, Alice Madonia, Igor Atake, Marta Azzolin, Lara Carosso
Venue: Frontiers in Marine Science
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2026.1936698
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The lack of spatially explicit, observation-grounded predictions for the transport and coastal deposition of floating marine macro-litter (FMML) in the Mediterranean.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A data-driven stochastic Lagrangian framework using Parcels, initialized with monthly gridded FMML observations from shipboard surveys and forced by Copernicus Marine Service Mediterranean reanalysis currents and ERA5 wind fields with a 1% windage coefficient and a 2D random-walk turbulent diffusio…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Mediterranean Sea, specifically areas surveyed via the LIFE Conceptu Maris Project using ferries from August 2023 to December 2024.
Abstract:
Introduction The Mediterranean is a major hotspot for floating marine macro-litter (FMML) accumulation, yet spatially explicit, observation-grounded predictions of its transport and coastal deposition remain scarce. We present a data-driven stochastic Lagrangian framework that uses monthly gridded FMML observations from systematic shipboard surveys as simulation initial conditions complementing existing source-based modelling approaches. Methods Observations were collected from August 2023 to December 2024 within the LIFE Conceptu Maris Project using ferries as monitoring platforms under a standardised protocol. A total of 158 surveys detected 4,801 FMML items across approximately 6,200 km² of surveyed sea surface, of which more than 62% were artificial polymers. Observed monthly FMML item counts at 5 × 5 km resolution initialised ensemble Lagrangian simulations (18 members per target month; 17.2–32.5 million virtual particles per seeding window, 5,000 particles per observed item) using Parcels, forced by Copernicus Marine Service Mediterranean reanalysis currents and ERA5 wind fields with a 1% windage coefficient and a 2D random-walk turbulent diffusion scheme. Monthly frequency-of-occurrence maps were computed at the sea surface and on coastlines. Results The Southern Tyrrhenian and Northern Ligurian seas, including the Pelagos Sanctuary, exhibited in 2024 near-persistent high sea surface FMML occurrence, peaking in late summer–autumn and reaching a seasonal minimum in winter–early spring. The Balearic Sea showed elevated occurrence from late spring through summer (May–September), declining through autumn. The Adriatic displayed intense sub-basin-scale spreading from January to June and again in December, with summer leakage into the Northern Ionian Sea. Coastal deposition frequencies were highest on Corsica, western Sardinia and northern Tunisia, then the south-eastern Tyrrhenian and Ligurian–Tuscan margins, with Valencia–Barcelona largely confined to summer. Integration with loggerhead turtle nesting records illustrates how coastal frequency-of-occurrence maps can support conservation applications. Discussion A web-based Particle Analysis Dashboard translates these outputs into an interactive tool with Marine Protected and Conserved Area overlays for scientists and decision-makers. The framework provides a scalable, observation-anchored foundation for MSFD Descriptor 10 monitoring, transferable to other semi-enclosed sea basins. Priority future work includes complementary validation against independent beach-litter monitoring data, integration of land-based source inventories, and linkage with species distribution models.
